utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. At the outset of today's hearing, the Chamber would like to deal with some procedural matters. First, the Chamber notes that the Prosecution has filed its notification of withdrawal of its motion concerning scheduling of Prosecution Rule 98 bis oral arguments on the 30th of June, 2011. This is hereby put on the record. Secondly, we are now very close to the end of the Prosecution's case, and the Trial Chamber needs to plan the next phase of the trial, as far as possible. Therefore, we would like the Prosecution to file a schedule for the remaining witnesses. The Trial Chamber notes that the confidential supplemental motion for leave to amend its 65 ter exhibit list and witness list, filed on the 14th of June, contains a request for the addition of two witnesses to the 65 ter witness list, and that this motion is still pending because we are awaiting B/C/S translation and then the response by the accused. So the schedule to be filed may need to be revised, in light of the decision of the Trial Chamber on this motion. Nonetheless, it will be helpful if the Prosecution files already a schedule of the remainder of the witnesses it now knows that it will be calling. May I ask the Prosecution, Mr. McCloskey, when you will be in a position to file the schedule?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This afternoon, Mr. President. I, of course, knew that that would be an interest for the Trial Chamber, and, of course, it's our interest -- everyone's interest, so I can go over it briefly to give you an idea. And I know Mr. Thayer is working on the filing, and even -- and an e-mail before that, so you can see it. But this last week, we have had a chance to, well, either get or not get witnesses, so I can give you briefly right now -- it won't take long so you can see where we are. It would probably be best to go into private session just because I will mention some witnesses' names, which I think is always helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We go into private session. I would appreciate such an update.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to raise two matters before you get the floor, Mr. McCloskey. We understand, from your submission just in private session, that you will be able to file such a schedule this afternoon, and we will be happy to receive it at least by tomorrow. Thank you. The Chamber would also request the Prosecution to -- I would like to put it in a different way. Was that already a withdrawal of certain witnesses from the 65 ter witness list or will it be part of your submission to be expected this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that would be part of the submission. I think it's the simplest way to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. At this point in time, I would like to ask you, Mr. Tolimir: The Trial Chamber would like to receive information on your future intentions to assist us in planning, if you are in a position to provide this information. As I said, we are now very close to the end of the Prosecution's case. Are you able to say whether you will be making submissions pursuant to Rule 98 bis, or will you be able to do that at a later stage? And if so, when can we expect that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please move the microphone. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I greet all those present, and may today's procedure be conducted in accordance with God's will and not mine. I would like to greet everyone, because I haven't seen any of you in a while. That includes the OTP, the Defence, and the Trial Chamber. I can say immediately after the end of the Prosecution case, the Defence will be ready to respond pursuant to Rule 98 bis, but that's following the break and following the end of the OTP's case. And we also shall be requiring some time to prepare. We don't have time to prepare while we're still busy hearing and cross-examining witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To avoid any misunderstanding, it's not a question to respond pursuant to Rule 98 bis, but if you will submit a motion according to Rule 98 bis. It's up to you to decide if you will file such a submission, oral submission in court, or not. And this is the question I wanted to put to you, if we can expect that or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. The Defence would like that to be in writing, if the Chamber so decides and, indeed, allows. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First, I would like to draw your attention to the wording of Rule 98 bis. It refers solely to oral submissions. I would understand that you prepare it in writing and then present it to the Chamber orally by reading it, but this is the wording of the Rule, itself. Again, I would like to ask you: Can you help us with any information, if you will be, and whether you will be, and, if so, when you will be in a position to tell us if there will be any 98 bis submission by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We shall certainly abide by your instructions and put forward our position orally, once we have it prepared. We can do that immediately after the Prosecution case is over. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That helps, and we understood your position. I would like now to turn to an additional matter. I would like to take the opportunity to remind the parties that there are currently many exhibits in evidence which only have draft translations. The Chamber invites both parties to up-load the final translations of the exhibits, once they are received, and to inform the Registry and the Chamber once this has taken place. By the end of this case, there should be no more draft translations in evidence. Mr. McCloskey, you wanted to raise another matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It was related to the previous discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then I just -- as I said, Ms. Stewart has given me, and I have a list of about 25 translations, if you would like me to read that into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To save some time, I would propose a different approach. You have provided the Chamber, by e-mail, with this list of 25 exhibits now with a translation into B/C/S or English. There's only one problem. The 15th exhibit, P2346, was MFI'd not only pending translation, but also for further authentication, so in that case this will not be admitted now, but depends on the further development of our case. All others should be -- there should be a list on the record by internal memorandum to save some time and possible misunderstandings. I would like to instruct the Registrar to provide the parties and the Chamber with such a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Any other matters to be raised? It's not the case. The witness should be brought in, please. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we just please go into private session for a moment? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The witness should be brought in now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please switch on the microphones. Good afternoon, sir. Welcome to the courtroom. Our apologies for the delayed start. We had to deal with some procedural matters. Would you now please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. First, the Prosecution, during their examination-in-chief, will put questions to you. Mr. Elderkin, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you, and good afternoon to Your Honours and everyone else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And to you, Witness. Could I ask, as we discussed when we met yesterday, that if it seems like we're going too fast, to try to speak at a pace that the interpreters can keep up with. And first of all, sir, please, could you say your full name?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, General. Good afternoon to the Prosecution. My name is Mile Micic. And do you want me to say anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And your father's name, please?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: My father's name is Marko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What's your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: 3rd November 1973. I was born in Zenica municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And you consider yourself to be of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, have you had a chance this weekend to look over the transcript of an interview that you gave to Prosecution investigators in November of 2009?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When you re-read your interview, did you identify any of your answers that were not correctly transcribed?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: There were a lot of grammatical errors. There were sentences that did not convey the proper sense, but that was, more or less, that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And apart from those grammatical errors, are all the answers that you gave during that interview accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: I did not understand your question. Could you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Are the answers recorded in the transcript accurate, in terms of the substantive information that you gave during the interview?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did you answer truthfully the questions that you were asked during that interview?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like to ask briefly about your education and background, to give the Court some sense of what happened in your life, before we move to 1995. First, could you tell us, briefly, what level of education you received?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Elementary and secondary education in my native municipality. The secondary school I attended was the School for Electricians, and that was what I completed before 1981 -- 1991. Then the war started. My education was thus interrupted, and I don't have any military education.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And what's your current occupation, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Currently, I'm a repairman. I repair electrical appliances in a factory, or, rather, electrical machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you ever perform military service?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: I didn't serve in the former JNA. I did my compulsory military service in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What date did you start your military service in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you serve in any particular VRS unit?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: It was the 67th Communications Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did you receive any specialist training when you joined the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you receive any specialist training beyond the training given to every soldier who joined the VRS? Did you learn any specialist skill or were you simply taught how to wear a uniform, to march, to fire a gun, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Besides the basic skills, I also had some training in communications specific to that regiment. That training was very short and didn't last more than a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What place were you when you received that training in the Communications Regiment?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: That training was carried out in the Communications Regiment, and its command was in Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: After you completed that training, did you continue to serve at Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What were your duties, during the period after you completed training, in 1992 through to, say, the end of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: When I completed the training, I started driving the commander and the deputy commander in my regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us their names, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: The commander's name was Lieutenant-Colonel Gredo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And at some point, did you become the driver to General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: That happened either in early 1995 or in mid-1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were you General Tolimir's driver before July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did you work full time as General Tolimir's driver once you were assigned to him?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you work only for General Tolimir, as his driver, once you were assigned to him, or did you perform additional tasks or other duties for the Communications Regiment at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: I did not have any assignments or duties in the regiment. My only task was to drive. And in this particular case, I drove the general. And I was also supposed to carry out his orders, if there were any forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Just to give us an idea of the work you did for General Tolimir, can you tell us what kind of car or cars General Tolimir was using at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: It was a small passenger vehicle, and there was also a jeep.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And were you responsible for maintaining those vehicles, or you simply would get in at the beginning of each day and do the driving, and that's it?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: My primary task was to drive. I also maintained the cars, making sure that nothing happened either to me or to the general while I was driving him around.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like to see, please, in e-court Exhibit P104, at page 10, I think, in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So while this image is coming up: As you'll remember, we looked yesterday at a simplified map, and I'd ask that when it comes on screen, you'll tell me if you agree that it shows the main roads in the eastern part of Republika Srpska. If we could rotate 90 degrees to the right, please, and perhaps you could zoom in first onto the top half and then scroll down after a moment, just so the writing is a little clearer. So are you able to make out the place names written on that map, and do you agree that it's a version of the map we had a look at yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, you showed me this map yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to leave that on screen while I move to July of 1995. It hopefully will help us as we talk through any of the trips we discuss. You told us you were General Tolimir's driver starting at some point in 1995, before July. Thinking now to July 1995, do you recall on what date Srebrenica was captured?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: I only heard in the media that that happened on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Why do you remember that particular date, the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: On that day, on the 12th of July, it was an important date for me because it is my Name Day celebration. Every person of Orthodox belief has such a day in a year. For me, it's the 12th of July. That's why I remember it so well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were you with General Tolimir on the 12th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: In the statement that I provided to you, I said that I remember that on the 12th of July, we went to Bijeljina and back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: To be clear for the record on this trial, because we haven't got your statement in evidence before the Court, you say: "We went to Bijeljina and back." Who do you mean by "we," please?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: General Tolimir and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So starting from the beginning of that day, can you tell us what you and General Tolimir did that day? Tell us about this trip to Bijeljina that you just mentioned. Where did you start from and how did you travel?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact time when we departed. We did not have any problems getting to Bijeljina. We arrived there. The general had some commitments over there. I don't know what those commitments were. It was not my duty to know. My duty was only to transport the general to the place where he told me to take him and to await further instructions. On that same day, we returned to Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You say you went to Bijeljina, and Bijeljina is a town. Was there a specific location in the town, a military location, or another facility that you went to on General Tolimir's order?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: I believe that I took him to the Security Department of the East Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Security Department at the East Bosnia Corps, what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: The general, I suppose, had a meeting. I don't know what. And I was waiting for him in a room which was a dedicated room for the drivers. That's where I usually waited for him. And he finished whatever he was doing, he came to me and he said, Let's go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were there any other drivers waiting with you in that room for their bosses to attend the same meeting? Do you know who else was at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: I don't know who else attended the meeting. I believe that only a soldier, whose duty was to make coffees, was in that same room with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If we could look at the map that we had on the screen a moment ago, if that's still available.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And so if we can scroll up the map, you see the red triangle in the centre. Hopefully that will come back in a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Carrying on scrolling down a little further, please. That's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, do you see, in the centre bottom of the picture, a red triangle marking Crna Rijeka? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us if the roads shown on this map, going up through Han Pijesak, then Vlasenica, Milici, past Zvornik, and then if we scroll further north, up along the river through Janja and up to Bijeljina, is that the route that you followed to go up for the meeting in Bijeljina on the 12th of July or was there another route that you followed?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: That's the only road that was passable at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And you told us after the meeting, you travelled back from Bijeljina to Crna Rijeka. Did you follow that same route back, as you say it's the only route passable at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you stop somewhere on the way back?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: I've already stated that we may have had a very short break in Vlasenica, perhaps a few minutes. I don't know exactly how long we stopped for, but it couldn't have been long.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So where in Vlasenica did you stop? Again, it's a town. Did you stop at a military facility, some other place in Vlasenica? Please be specific.

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: We stopped in front of the corps command building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, after the 12th of July, for the rest of that month, do you remember any other specific dates or the events of any other specific dates on which you drove General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, without trying to establish specific dates, in which area were you driving General Tolimir during the rest of that month, which part of the country?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: One day, we travelled to Zepa -- actually, to one part of the area between Rogatica and Zepa. However, I can't remember what date was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And I don't want to ask you about trying to establish a specific date if you can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: But I would like to, please, have in e-court page 12 of the same exhibit, P104. If you could scroll down a little bit, please. I think like -- like that is good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So do you remember looking also at this map we have on the screen now when we met yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: There are various locations marked on this map, showing the area from Han Pijesak down to Rogatica. And as you can see, some of the place names are mentioned in English, but they all have the town, or village name, or another designation in the label which I hope you can understand. If we can look at the map in the area from Zepa and perhaps just further south from there, if we can scroll slightly further down. Sir, can you recall travelling to locations in this area when you say you went to Zepa sometime in July of 1995? And, specifically, we can see the locations marked there as "Boksanica Check-Point," "Borike IKM," and also "Borike Villa." Did you go to any of these locations in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the Boksanica check-point. That's where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And you said: "That's where we were." Just to be clear for the trial record, by "we," do you mean yourself and General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you spend any nights away from Crna Rijeka, in this area, during July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you stay at any location in this area, in the Borike area and Boksanica area, with General Tolimir or close by to General Tolimir during July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: By the Boksanica check-point, that's where the general and myself spent a few days. I don't know how many days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know of a place that's called here the Borike Villa? Have you heard of that place?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Is that a place or is that a feature or facility, Villa Borike? I've never heard of any such thing before. What is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know of a villa that used to be the property of, I think, Dzemal Bijedic located at Borike, a house, like a country house by a forest and by some open plains near the Borike Horse Farm?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: There was a building there. I don't know what it was called or who it belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Was it some kind of villa or country house?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: A building of some sort a bit more elaborate than just a normal, ordinary house. A bit more luxurious, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did General Tolimir, to your knowledge or recollection, spend any nights at that location while you were in the area in July of 1995? Did he sleep there?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: In one of the buildings, perhaps in that building - I don't remember - if memory serves me well, I think that we did spend one night in that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, sleep in the building or did you, as the driver, sleep somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: I spent that one evening in one of the buildings there. I'm not sure if that was the one or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment, Mr. Elderkin. Could you please describe the buildings, if you seen there, as you just indicated, at least more than one building; for instance, the size, the colour, and which they belonged to each other? Could you describe them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I said there was one building, as far as I remember, and I can't remember exactly how it looked. I can't remember any of the details. Perhaps it was a little -- its condition was a little better than the condition of an ordinary house would have been at the time, and that's about as much as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What do you think when this building, this house, was built, in which time-period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly before the war, I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before which war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The war that broke out in 1992 in BH territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was it built in the 19th century, or the 20th century, before or after the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure if I'm able to answer this question. Probably after World War II, but I don't know when exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you recall how many buildings were in these premises or nearby?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think just the one building. I can't remember any others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Elderkin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember which vehicle you were driving during this time you spent in the Borike and Boksanica area with General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Given the lay of the land, it was a jeep vehicle we were using, a Mercedes vehicle built specially for hilly terrain like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: This Mercedes jeep, was it fitted out for military use?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: It was the kind of car used by the former JNA, and it was now in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did it have any kind of communications capability, any kind of radio communication capability?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, during the same month, July 1995, did you ever go down into Zepa town?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, once. I can't remember the date or the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Who did you go with?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What did you do with General Tolimir down in Zepa town? Did you spend some time there or drive down and return immediately?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: I drove the general there. I waited up, perhaps half an hour or thereabouts, and then we drove back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Was the Muslim population still in Zepa while you were down there?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, some were still around; I'm not sure if all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that? I'm not sure if I'm clear about what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: The Muslim population, the people you observed in Zepa town while you were there, what were they doing? Were they preparing to leave? Were they simply going about their daily lives?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: They certainly weren't pursuing their day-to-day activities. Were they preparing to leave? I can't say, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you witness any convoy leaving Zepa to take the Muslim population to other parts of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see one of those convoys with citizens leaving the area. It took them an awfully long time to leave the area, given the conditions that prevailed at the time, and the road was in very poor condition. There was some buses that would break down along the road, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you play any part in travelling with this convoy? Tell us about what you remember.

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Well, I had no part to play in that. My only task was to wait and to carry out any orders by the general, drive him places whenever that was required, and that was the only job I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where did you drive when you left Zepa town?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question. Where, when I left Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you ever drive from Zepa to the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, from Zepa we went back to the check-point, and that's where we stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to ask you about accompanying or leading a convoy from Zepa to the confrontation line. Do you remember talking about that subject in the interview that you reviewed yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: I remember that one occasion, I believe. I was driving a car. General Tolimir was in it and another person. I don't know who. In my opinion, we were at the head of the column, I think the second car at the head, preceded by the police at the head and the tail of the column securing the column. So we were the number-two car in that column. My task or my role - at least that is my opinion - was to go all the way to the end of that route so that this person who was driving with us would make sure that the convoy got through safe and that everyone would be fine as they were on their way through RS territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When you got to the end of that route, where did you return afterwards? I assume you didn't stay at the edge of RS territory.

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: Again, again, as far as the confrontation line. When the people or population left, we drove back to Boksanica, the check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you make this journey to the confrontation line and back only one time or on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILE MICIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly whether it was once or twice. At any rate, it wasn't more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Thank you very much. Those are all the questions that I have, and I put myself in the Judges' hands. I believe it's General Tolimir's turn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Elderkin. Now Mr. Tolimir has the opportunity to put questions to you, sir. Mr. Tolimir, it's your turn now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Again, peace to all of you, and may God steer us in our proceedings here. I wish Mr. Micic a very good day, I wish him a pleasant stay in here Den Haag, and a safe trip back home. And I would like to thank him for coming here to testify. I have no questions for him. The one thing that I'd like to say is I'm exceptionally pleased to see him. He's done his job. He's done what he was expected to do. Thank you very much, sir. I have no questions for this witness. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, I take it since there was no cross-examination, there will be no re-examination by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct, Your Honour. If I may also note, I don't know whether our next witness has yet been brought across. We were expecting a little longer on cross-examination. But if we could start the break now, and we can try and sort things out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, you will be pleased that this concludes your examination here in this trial, in this courtroom. Now you are free to return to your normal residence and your normal activities. The Chamber would like to thank you that you were able to come to The Hague and testify in this trial. Indeed, I think it's appropriate to have our first break now, and I hope that the next witness will be ready after the break. We adjourn and resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, especially to you, Ms. Hasan. Welcome back. The witness should be brought back in, please. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Before the witness comes in, I completed my questioning of the last witness without asking any questions because I know that he still suffers from traumas after losing his father and his brother. I could tell that he was under a lot of stress. I also felt that Mr. Elderkin was about to ask him more questions. I don't oppose his statement being admitted, where he provides a more detailed account of everything that went on. It might be useful to both us and the OTP. I conferred with my legal counsel, and he has informed me that the statement has not been admitted. It's 1D114. And he clearly pointed out -- the witness clearly pointed out that he stood by that statement. Therefore, I think it might as well be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the moment, I can only note that it is too late for such a submission. We are dealing now with the next witness. Good afternoon, sir. Welcome to the courtroom. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. The Prosecution is now putting questions to you. Ms. Hasan now has the floors.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good afternoon witness. Good afternoon to everyone else in the courtroom. Just one preliminary matter, and that is that I was informed by the witness this morning that he suffers from a medical condition that prevents him for sitting down for long periods of time. Particularly, he has told me -- he has advised that after approximately an hour to an hour and a half, he starts feeling -- experiencing pain in his legs, and so it may be the case that he may need a break during his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this information. Indeed, I would like to invite you to indicate whenever there is a need for a break, you should tell us and then we will do that, so that there is no reason for any pain for you. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, would you please state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Mihajlo Galic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Have you recently had an opportunity to listen to the testimony that you gave in 2007 in the Popovic et al case?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Was the evidence that you gave during your testimony in 2007 true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I listened to it, and as far as I remember, the account was the most truthful that I could provide at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So if I asked you those very same questions today, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I then offer the transcript of Mr. Galic's testimony from the Popovic case, bearing 65 ter number 6564 - that's the under-seal transcript - and 65 ter 6565, to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Both exhibits will be received, the former under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 6564 shall be assigned Exhibit P2436, under seal, and 65 ter document 6565 shall be assigned Exhibit P2437. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And as regards the exhibits that were admitted through this witness or used with him during his prior testimony, there are a number of them that have already been admitted in this case. For those that have not been, they have -- a few of them have already been assigned P numbers, provisional P numbers, and I will read those out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think there is no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is a very long list, and I take it it starts with P1107, MFI, and goes to P1125, MFI.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Those who are not yet in evidence will be admitted, and the Registrar will provide you with -- no, there is no need. We have already the P numbers as MFI'd. I would like to ask the Registrar to consult with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: As they already have provisional P numbers, there is no need for an internal memorandum. All those listed will be received. There's only one which has not a P number yet. This is 65 ter 7091. This will be received and given a P number by the Registrar now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7091 shall be assigned Exhibit P2438.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I ask you, have all the exhibits a translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe I see here one, P1114, does not appear to have a translation, which we will provide in due course, and I don't see any other ones. There is one note, and that's in respect to P1115 -- sorry, it seems that there's more than just P1114 that requires a translation; P1116 and P1117, as well as 1118, so more than the one I first referred to. In addition, P1115 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To avoid any error or misunderstanding at a later stage, I would like to invite you to file a note to the Registry. They will provide you and the parties and the Chamber with an internal memorandum indicating which one of these documents are only marked for identification, pending translation, and those who are already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Certainly. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I will then now move to read a summary of this witness's prior testimony. In July of 1995, Mihajlo Galic was a major and the assistant chief of staff for Reinforcement and Personnel Affairs of the Zvornik Brigade and worked directly under the chief of staff and deputy commander, Major Dragan Obrenovic. On the evening of the 13th of July, at approximately 10.00 or 11.00 p.m., Mr. Galic was resting at the Zvornik Brigade Command when he received instructions to go to the brigade's forward command post, the brigade's IKM, in Kitovnica, to replace Zvornik Brigade chief of security, Lieutenant Drago Nikolic as the IKM duty officer. Nikolic was not present at the IKM when Mr. Galic arrived, and Mr. Galic did not try to contact him. Mr. Galic arrived at the IKM on the night of the 13th of July in advance of his scheduled shift which was to commence at 7.00 in the morning on the 14th of July. Mr. Galic remained on duty at the IKM until the morning of the 15th of July. He testified that his replacement of Nikolic on the night of the 13th of July was an "extraordinary shift duty." During his testimony, Mr. Galic was shown the original IKM log-book. He confirmed that he wrote the 13th of July, 1995, entry and that the signature was his. In addition to testifying about replacing Nikolic at the brigade's IKM, Mr. Galic also testified about a number of other topics, including: the presence of the Zvornik Brigade's commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Vinko Pandurevic's presence in the field from 4th or 5th July until at least the 15th of July; an order that he passed on from Pandurevic to the Zvornik Brigade's assistant chief of staff for Operations and Training, Major Miodrag Dragutinovic, regarding Dragutinovic's next assignment; the number of Serb soldiers who were killed in the Baljkovica area during the 15th and 16th of July, in 1995, before the opening of the corridor; as well as his knowledge concerning Exhibit P1112 of instructions which the brigade received from the Main Staff in 1994 regarding the security organ reporting procedures.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. Galic, you have heard the summary I have just read about your prior testimony. Are there any changes you would like to make to that or does that accurately give a fair representation of the testimony you gave?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: This is precisely what I stated. Your words were an accurate reflection of what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no questions for this witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, are you in a position to commence your cross-examination now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May God's will be done in these proceedings, and not necessarily mine. I would like to greet the witness and wish him a pleasant stay in our midst. We'll start with the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the summary, the Prosecutor said that you were on furlough from the brigade and that later on you were sent to the forward command post to relieve Drago Nikolic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I already at this point in time ask both speakers to pause between question and answer, wait a moment, because everything has to be interpreted into our language so that there's no overlapping. Please continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question. Please, could you tell us who was it who ordered you to go to the forward command post and be on duty there?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I was on furlough, which means that the duty officer approached me and told me to go to the forward command post and do what I did. So I received that information or that was conveyed to me by the brigade duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the duty officer receive that order from his superior or from his subordinate? Thank you. Could you please wait until the moment my words are fully recorded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know who he received the order or the message from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In this part of the summary, the Prosecutor said that that was an extraordinary shift duty. Did you perform extraordinary shift duty at that command post before and after that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes. For me, that was an extraordinary shift duty because I was not on the rota. Before that and after that, I was on the rota of the brigade command. I was assigned to work as a duty officer at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your chief of staff, who was your immediate superior, know that you were supposed to go to the IKM to relieve Drago Nikolic of his duty? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I didn't know it then; I don't know it now. I don't know whether he knew that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the witness please be shown -- and we have to move into private session in order to use the evidence provided by Witness PW-057. Can we go into private session, or if somebody thinks that we can stay in open session, I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have page 7 of the Serbian and page 8 of the English so that everyone is able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see here Attorney Petrusic saying "Zvornika Brigada" had a single military police company. And then your answer is: "Yes." And then the question is: "Who was in command of that military police contingent?" And then Mihajlo Galic answers: "The military police commander, and you see this unit was directly subordinate to the security organ." He goes on to say: "Hence, we may conclude and move this to the level of the personnel issue; that the company commander was Miomir Jasikovac in July 1995, while his superior officer along this line of command was Drago Nikolic." And your answer is: "That's right." My question to you, sir, is this: Do you know who was Jasikovac's superior, and who had the authority to issue orders to Jasikovac? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: The company commander. The commander, the chief of staff, or the security chief could have issued an order to the commander of the Military Police Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What you just said, is that in keeping with the rules on the use of the military police? Thank you. ^

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I answer to the best of my ability and knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for what you said. Do you know who exercises command over a military police unit that is part of a brigade? Who writes up its assessment? Who punishes them? Who rewards them? You were a personnel officer, so would this happen, Drago Nikolic or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: All the units within the brigade are under the brigade commander. Nevertheless, the chief of security is the person or the officer who works closely with the military police, as far as I know, and he gets military policemen to perform all sorts of tasks; security, escort control, arresting people, securing a compound, military barracks, that sort of thing. That's as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. A while ago when I read that thing in closed session, did you not see that Mr. Nikolic was demanding that Mr. Obrenovic place at his disposal Mr. Jasikovac and a component of the military police? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, and I remember that the unit was already engaged in combat at that point in time, if my understanding is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see that later on in that conversation, he said, I'll think about it, when the other man wants to have at least a part of that unit, and then he says, I'll think about it. So my question is: First of all, did you hear that, when Obrenovic told Nikolic, I'll think about it, whether I'll give you at least a part of that unit?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that from you because you read it back to me. It really depends on what each of them were busy doing at the time, so that's probably why he phrased the remark the way he did, but not that I'd know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If Drago Nikolic had been in command of that unit, would he have asked permission from Obrenovic or would he have done as he saw fit?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Some of the activities performed within the military police company, I know that Drago Nikolic deployed those people outside the barracks, inside the barracks, getting them there, sending them elsewhere. Did he do that of his own initiative or with someone's approval is not something that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it perhaps the commander who ordered him to deploy these people, in keeping with an order by the commander, himself? Is this something that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that a commander commands the military police, they are directly subordinate to him, just like in the case of battalion commanders in other units that are part of a brigade? Do you know that? You were a personnel officer, after all. That's why I'm asking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: As a matter of principle, all the units are linked to the commander, and the commander commands these units, but there are probably some situations when the authorities shift. I'm not familiar with the rules governing the work of the military police, and I'm not privy to all the nuts and bolts of how this actually worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that you don't understand. It's not your job. There is stuff that we don't know about your work.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But can we please now look at P1297, which is the rules governing the work of the military police. It's about to come up on the screen. This is the rules governing the work of the military police in the Armed Forces of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you tendering the previous document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 1D915 will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D915 shall be assigned Exhibit D294. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At this point in time, I would like to draw your attention to another problem. The testimony of the witness in the Popovic case was -- these transcripts were already assigned with P numbers, but I give the floor to the Registrar to have it on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave, the transcript of Mihajlo Galic's testimony in the Popovic et al case, dated 25th to 27th April, 2007, was already assigned two exhibit numbers, one to the confidential version, P1105, and P01106 to the public redacted version of the transcript. Further to that, exhibit numbers assigned today, namely, P2436, under seal, to the 65 ter document 6564, and P2437 to the 65 ter document 6565, shall be removed, to be assigned to some other Prosecution documents yet to be tendered. In light of this correction, Exhibit P2438 that was assigned to the 65 ter document 7091 will also be assigned to another document at a later stage. At this point, Exhibit P2436 will be reassigned to the 65 ter document 7091. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this correction. Sir, I would like to remind you again, if you need a break, please let us know. Otherwise, Mr. Tolimir will continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We may continue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we please now have the title of these rules so the witness can see it. Thank you. Page 2 in e-court in the English. Could we please now look at item 12 or paragraph 12, which is page 13 in the Serbian and page 10 in the English - thank you - paragraph 12. Thank you. Could we please go to page 9 in the Serbian. This is page 20. Nothing for us there. Paragraph 12 of the rules. Thank you. That's Chapter 2. Thank you very much. Could you please zoom in a little so the witness can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, I'm about to quote, for your benefit, paragraph 12 of these rules. Before that, let me ask you: Do you know if, in your brigade of the VRS, the rules for the former JNA were, indeed, used? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. There were no other rules that we could use, at least not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Please have a look at paragraph 12. Chapter 2, "The Command and Control of the Military Police," that is the heading. Number 12 reads: "The officer in charge of the military unit, and institution within whose establishment the military police unit is placed or to which it is attached, commands and controls the military police." My question: Who would be the officer in charge of the military police, in keeping with paragraph 12 of these rules? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Based on this, based on what you read out in paragraph 12, it would be the most senior brigade commander. But, again, I have to stress this: I find myself analysing these rules and instructions governing the work of the military police. I've never read this previously, nor, indeed, was I at any point in time familiar with this. It's very difficult for me to address anything at all in relation to this set of rules that I was never familiar with, to begin with. The evidence that I provided was based on my impressions of how things worked at the time back in 1992 -- 1991 through 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise to you, sir, but given your statement, the statement that we have just quoted, saying that Drago Nikolic was in command, I wish to ask you now this, sir: Under the rules, could the commander have been Drago Nikolic or would it have had to be the brigade commander? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Based on what we see on the screen, no. But then whenever there's a rule, there must be an exception too, so this was probably one of those occasional exceptions where someone had to be in command, regardless of what the rules actually said. I'm not sure if my understanding is correct, but this is what the rules say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We'll get to those exceptions. Thank you very much. Let's move on to paragraph 13 to see whether that constitutes an exception: "With respect to specialty, the officer in charge of the security body of the unit or institution within whose establishment the military police unit is placed or to which it is attached controls the military police. He makes suggestions to the officer in charge of the military unit or institution on the use of military police units and is responsible for the combat readiness of the military police unit and the performance of their tasks." End of quote. My question: Based on the provisions of paragraph 13, the commander remains the same, but the security organ makes suggestions on the use of the military police units; is that what the rules say?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: It's not up to me to change the rule I see before my very eyes, and I can't change what I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to paragraph 2 of Article 13: "When controlling a military police unit, the officer in charge of the security body," from the first paragraph of this article, from paragraph 1 of this item, "has the same rights and duties which the officers of arms services of military units and institutions have in controlling the units of arms and services." My question: Did Drago Nikolic have the same rights as the chief -- the various chiefs, the artillery chief, the engineers chief, the signals chief, or were his rights any different under these provisions of this article.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I simply don't know. I'm simply unable to interpret these rules, and it follows that I don't know how to answer your question as to whether he had the same rights or different rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I understand you. As a personnel officer working in a brigade, did you know who exercised command over whom and who was who else's superior officer?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I was familiar with the organisation chart of the brigade. I knew what the links were between people, but I can't be more specific about any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What about those charts that you used? Was there a link between the military police commander and the brigade commander or the military police commander and the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Sir, General, it wasn't my chart. I just looked at it several times, but I wasn't the one who produced it or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us this: What about the personnel organ; did it have a working chart listing all the assistant commanders and all the lower-ranking commanders that were directly in touch with the overall commander? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: The personnel unit had the brigade's establishment chart. We had all the records, and those were the documents that we had. I'm not sure what to call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What did the establishment chart say? Were the links drawn there between who was -- as to who was directly in touch with whom?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I don't remember specifically, but I think that the number of people in the command, in the units, in terms of their military specialties, in terms of their ranks, were all there, and that's how it was regulated. Each unit had a certain number of this, a certain number of that, a certain number of men. I was only interested in the number of men because that's what my records were about, the ones that I was keeping, but I didn't know about the links between these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As it was you who would deliver to the commander for signature proposals or decisions regarding promotions -- or, rather, did you do that? When someone else was promoted to a higher rank or a higher position, did you submit those documents for signature to the commander, and how exactly did you do that? Can you tell the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: When officers were promoted under the brigade commander, the brigade commander would be in charge of that. Whenever there was something that was wasn't within his remit, it would be left to the superior commands; the corps command, for example. Therefore, as far as I remember, this was broken up for officers, for NCOs, and a different procedure applied in each of these cases. I think the officers were under their superior commands -- under the brigade commander and the NCOs under their superior commands. That's as much as I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you remember who made the proposals for these promotions to a higher rank or a higher position? Who was in charge of the proposals? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was the units who made those proposals based on the results of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since the units proposed that, tell me, who was in charge of promotions for commanders of independent units in the brigade? And could you also tell us which of the independent units existed in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Proposals for the promotion of the officers of independent units, I assume that it came -- they came from the chief of staff to the commander. And as for the independent units within the brigade, those were battalions, the Military Police Company, the Engineers Company and the Communications Company, as far as I can remember. It was a long time ago, so I'm not entirely sure that that was indeed the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It was, indeed, the way you have just told us. You have just mentioned a military police company. Was it directly linked to the brigade commander as an independent unit in the brigade? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: All units were linked to the brigade commander, all units. And if we follow that analogy, then the answer would be, Yes. However, there were exceptions. I remember that the Military Police Company was also linked to the chief of security, according to the schematic. That's how it was supposed to be. I don't know whether that was, indeed, the case, whether it was really true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you show that schematic to the lawyers, or the Prosecutor, or the Judges when you testified? Was that schematic presented, as such, to corroborate your words?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't have that schematic. I never had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, this is a tribunal. It's very important for the Trial Chamber to know whether the military police was an independent unit, subordinated to the commander, or was it subordinated to somebody else. This is a tribunal. It's very important for you to remember and to tell us, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I can only remember that all units were the commander's responsibility. The commander was responsible for all the units. That's as much as I know. Anything else I would tell you, I would go beyond that way of thinking, because the commander was responsible for all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at the bullet point 13 that you see on the screen, where it says: "The military police, in professional terms, is controlled by the officer of the security organ of the military unit or institution on whose strength it exists." Does the security organ command or control the military police unit? There is a big difference there.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: This is what it says. I can't change that. I don't know it. I can't change anything, if that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what control, in professional terms, is, and does it differ from the function of command when we talk about the military police?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: The terms "control" and "command," I don't know what the two mean exactly. I don't know the difference between "control" and "command." I don't know whether the two are the same or not. When it says, with respect to speciality, the officer in charge of the security body of the unit or institution within whose establishment the military police unit is placed controls the military police, I can't explain that. I don't know the difference between "control" and "command."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you're not in a position to do that, can you look at bullet points 12 and 13, and can you conclude who is it who commands, on the one hand, and who is it who controls?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I can only read what it says in here. According to bullet point 12, it says here that: "The officer in charge of the military unit and institution within whose establishment the military police unit is placed or to which it is attached commands and controls ..." And then in bullet point 13, it just mentions controls. These two things obviously are different. There is a distinction, but I'm not aware of it. It's very difficult for me to make a distinction between bullet point 12 and bullet point 13. Really, I'm not in a position to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is this: Bullet point 12 speaks about command. Does bullet point 13 speak only about professional control or does it also speak about command? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Bullet point 12 speaks about command and control, whereas bullet point 13 speaks about specialty and professional control, as far as I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. There's no need to belabour that point. Let's look at P1111, which is a document that you, yourself, drew up in your previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up P1111. Thank you. Can this be zoomed in a little. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you draw this up yourself, this schematic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't draw it up. It was readily available and made available to me. I only entered the names of people who discharged certain duties. Somebody asked me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And is this schematic correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't answer whether it is correct or not. This was given to me to fill out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And now look at where it says "Staff" and then "Chief of Staff." And you indicate that the Military Police Company was also under his command. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I did not understand you. What are you asking me? Below the "Chief of Staff," what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes. Do you see a list of subordinated assistants, headed by you, and does the second column also display the Military Police Company and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the "Military Police Company" here, but I'm looking at the following page as well or the other part of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please encircle, in red pen, where you see the "Military Police Company"? Was it subordinated to the chief of staff or not? In other words, is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether this correct or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please wait a moment. The Court Usher will assist you. You were asked to encircle the words "Military Police Company."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks] There in two places, here and here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you have encircled the "Military Police Company" on the right-hand-side, is this your handwriting where it says the "Military Police Company" and "Jasikovac"?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my handwriting, and at that moment I thought that that was how things had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please put number 1 next to the Cyrillic upper-case "Military Police Company" and number 2 to the same words handwritten by you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now -- no, no. No, no. Can we scroll up to see who signed this schematic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, this is not possible. If you move it, you will lose the markings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted? And then we will move the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This marked scheme will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit P1111 that was marked by the witness in court shall be assigned Exhibit D295. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would suggest, for the benefit of the witness, that we have our second break now so that the last session will be one hour again, and we are now sitting for more than one hour. I think it's the best time to have the break now, and then you may continue. This marking is saved, and we have it in evidence. We must have our second break now, and we will resume after half an hour at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan. I see you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, there's just a preliminary matter before the witness is brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This part will be redacted. Don't mention the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Can we go into private session at this moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We go into private session, and the last part will be redacted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that there is no objection by the Prosecution to receive 1D914 into evidence. It will be received as an Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D914 shall be assigned Exhibit D296. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And there was another mistake. When we referred to a list of documents with the previous -- no, with the current witness, I referred to one document which was not previously assigned with a P number and MFI'd. I referred to the wrong one. Mr. Registrar should put the correction on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, from the list of MFI'd documents for which the translation was provided, namely, 65 ter document 7411, which was assigned Exhibit P2246, it's still to be marked for identification, pending further authentication by the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I hope we have now resolved all problems with numbering and others. This witness should be brought in again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome back to the courtroom, sir. Sorry for the delay. We had to deal with some procedural matters again. Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Gajic [as interpreted], please, let's look at P1111 again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you're right, Mr. Gajic. The current witness is Mr. Galic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Galic, we're looking at the schematic, and let's keep it as it is. Let's not move anything until we have explored this in detail. You tied only the battalions to the commander, the Rear Battalion, the Engineers, and the Communications Battalion. Everything else, according to you, was linked with the chief of staff; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: The horizontal line, the "Staff" and the rest, I suppose that this means this is a line that goes all the way to the commander, that everything is linked to the commander and everybody else, because there is a common line. That's at least what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And my next question, sir: Did you also think that the Military Police Company's linked to the chief of staff? Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: It says here that they were linked to the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it, indeed, the case? Was the company linked to the chief of staff or to the commander, as you just said it yourself?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: All units are linked to the commanders. I've already told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So is this a mistake, then. Was a mistake made when the Military Police Company was shown as being linked to the chief of staff? Did that unit report together with you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Did it report together -- what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please stop. Pause between question and answer. We didn't get the answer yet. Please put the question again, and then the witness may answer, but please pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Galic, could you please tell us, did you go to morning briefings to the chief of staff or to the commander? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: To both, both the commander and the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you please tell us: Why did you show the military police as attending briefings in the chief of staff's office? Why did you show them as being subordinated to the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I don't see a reference to any briefings. This is not to show how briefings were organised. I didn't know any better at the moment when I drew this up. I did it to the best of my abilities at the time according to what I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When it comes to briefings, are briefings organised by the superior officers; i.e., does a subordinate report to a superior?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: Yes, a subordinate reports to his superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, can you tell us: Who did the commander of the military police company report to? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, let's look at this schematic, at the words that you added by hand. You put the Military Police Company as being linked to the chief of security. Can you see that in the third vertical column, or the fourth, rather? Can you tell us whether the chief -- or, rather, whether the Military Police Company can be linked to both the commander and the chief of security? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC
utterances.text: It doesn't appear to be logical in this particular chart, but the idea was the chief of security was someone that the unit was with all the time, and he was with the units, and vice versa. So that's how it worked.
